> **Class of Water**: refers to the range of the approximate wet surface area and permeability of affected materials remaining within the drying environment at the time drying is initiated.

> **Class 1** – least amount of water absorption and will likely evaporate; materials are predominantly low porosity  
> **Examples** – water is retained on the surface, little or no wet carpet or cushion

> **Class 2** – significant amount of water absorption and evaporation load; water intrusion has flowed into the area and wet materials are medium to high porosity  
> **Examples** – carpet, gypsum wall board

> **Class 3** – greatest amount of water absorption and evaporation load; water intrusion where wet, porous materials represent majority of the combined floor, wall, and ceiling surface area in the space  
> **Examples** – carpet, gypsum wall and ceiling board

> **Class 4** – deeply held or bound water resulting in a low potential rate of evaporation after bulk water removal; affected materials are typically low in porosity or the building assemblies may require special methods, longer drying times, or substantial water vapor pressure differentials  
> **Examples** – plaster, hardwood, concrete, masonry, gym floors, structural cavities, stone, brick

The definitions come from **American National Standards Institute (ANSI)/IICRC S500-2015, Standard and Reference Guide for Professional Water Damage Restoration**.
